claims.text: A one-hour pre-oxidation treatment at 1100–1200 °C under low oxygen partial pressure will induce a protective oxide scale on the refractory high-entropy alloy.
The pre-formed scale will be CrTaO4-based and contain minor Al2O3 and Cr2O3.
The pre-formed scale will be uniform, dense, and adherent.
The pre-oxidation treatment will significantly reduce subsequent oxidation rates during extreme-temperature service.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys typically form non-uniform, porous, or otherwise non-protective scales during direct high-temperature oxidation.
A dense oxide scale can inhibit oxygen transport and thereby reduce oxidation rate.
The scale inhibits outward diffusion of oxygen and inward diffusion of metallic species.
The proposed pre-oxidation conditions promote rapid nucleation and growth of a stable surface oxide layer.
The pre-formed scale is denser and more adherent than the scale formed by direct oxidation of the untreated alloy.
The pre-formed scale will mitigate scale spallation during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
After exposure at 1100 °C in air for 100 hours, pre-oxidized samples will have lower mass gain than untreated samples.
After exposure at 1100 °C in air, pre-oxidized samples will retain a more uniform and adherent oxide layer than untreated samples.
The intervention is expected to work preferentially in refractory high-entropy alloys whose compositions favor CrTaO4 and related oxide formation.
The treatment's effectiveness may vary substantially with alloy composition and treatment atmosphere.
Thermal cycling may crack the engineered scale and reduce the intervention's effectiveness.
The degree of oxidation-rate reduction depends on precise control of the pre-oxidation parameters.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% statistically significant mass-gain reduction, or formation of a less uniform or more spallation-prone scale, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The structural-mediator field describes oxygen diffusion as outward and metallic-species diffusion as inward, whereas the mechanism identifies oxygen ingress as the harmful transport being suppressed. These descriptions assign inconsistent directions to the relevant oxidation transport processes.
